en: Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha: Rasendracintāmaṇi (RCint), 1

O Lord, salutations to You— the auspicious one who bestows the quality of detachment upon those whose limbs are smeared with ashes, the impeller, whose crest is adorned by the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of Smara, whose very nature is Śakti,

the Sovereign, the ocean of compassion, the giver of refuge, the treasury of knowledge, the one beyond attributes, the Lord of beings, the husband of Girijā, the bearer of the moon, the deity of auspiciousness!
I bow to the God worshipped by the hosts of deities, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the one who brings about the destruction of obstacles.
Those of noble mind who constantly remember [this] do not experience hardships; this is the truth.
By the command of Śiva, I compose this commentary on the *Rasendracintāmaṇi*, which is pure, filled with essence, and mixed with the *Siddhinandana*.
Now, the disciple of Kālanātha, named Śrī Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, commencing the work *Rasendracintāmaṇi*,

extols with words containing the essence of the specific Siddhānta the two root deities, the illustrious Ambikā and Maheśvara, who are the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire world.
I take refuge in the body of Śiva and Śivā, which consists of the lotus pond of discernment that illuminates all meanings, and which is the manifestation of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
It is called the *Cintāmaṇi* because, by virtue of its small size, it bestows knowledge of all flavors, just like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
I have heard from the mouths of the highly learned and have seen established in the treatises that which has not been composed; I do not write that here.
But that work which I performed before my mature gurus, that I declare here, free from hesitation. (RCint 1.4)
Those who are capable of teaching and demonstrating the deeds of the Lord of Sūtas are the true gurus;
those alone are the disciples who compose [works] before their guru, while the rest merely partake in the performance of both roles.
We indeed endeavor to make manifest those very formative forces (saṃskāra) which are hidden within the dependent nature (paratantra) and indicated as accomplishments (siddhi). RCint 1.6.
May the heat of our labor reduce to ashes the lineages of those who cite practical applications from this work or insert their own names within it—until the end of the age. RCint_1.7.
The ritual preparations for the birth of Śiva are of many kinds, some of which can be accomplished with little effort while others require great exertion.
If I were to describe only those that are easy to perform, what would be the point of mentioning the others hereafter? (RCint 1.8)

In this world, since suffering is an object of unconditioned aversion for a person, its absence must be desired; likewise, happiness must be sought because it is an object of unconditioned affection. These two constitute the human goals (puruṣārtha), as they are distinct from mere non-existence.
Furthermore, although objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women are causes of pleasure, they must be avoided because they are permeated by inseparable suffering,
because they are attended by a succession of calamities, because they appear like a poisoned fruit to fools, because they are non-exclusive (anaikāntika),
because they are not seen simultaneously with their opposites, and because they lack permanence. // RCint_1.10 //

Furthermore, these means—namely, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), the yoga of breath (*pavanayoga*), and the yoga of alchemy (*rasayoga*)—are indeed equal in their exclusivity and finality, just like Hari, Hara, and Brahmā. (RCint 1.11)
Now, in response to the inquiry as to how these two are equal, we cite the words of Vasiṣṭha in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna* within the *Mokṣopāya* (the *Vasiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa*) and other texts:
"Yoga is not attainable by everyone, nor is the certainty of knowledge;
therefore, the supreme Lord Śiva declared two distinct methods."
If you do not bring about the cessation of consciousness through either the suppression of the vital breaths or the stirring away of latent impressions,
then you are not a practitioner of yoga.
For these two, O Rāma— knowledge and yoga— are remembered as being truly equal.

In this regard, since the first two [methods] are somehow curable even for those whose afflictions (*kaṣāya*) have merely ripened, whereas the last one provides the qualification even for those who are greedy for worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), to whom would it not appear that this [last method] is the most excellent?

Furthermore, a few drops from this ocean of qualities—the King of Elixirs (*rasarāja*) of the Blessed One, which, as the essence of the Blessed One, brings about the production of all the constituent elements (*dhātu*) within his own followers—are here recorded by way of context:
"O Goddess, in a short time the body becomes free from old age and death."
And the concentration of the mind is attained through the application of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
O Goddess, he who consumes the impurity of death or birth attains vitality and consciousness preceded by knowledge; the mantras become effective for him as truth.
As long as there is no descent of power (śaktipāta) and as long as there is no severing of the bonds (pāśakṛntana),
how can purification arise for him during the impurity caused by death or birth?
As long as one does not consume the seed of Hara— the mercury (rasa)—
how can there be liberation for him, and how can there be the maintenance of the physical body?
O beloved, practice constantly that knowledge of mercury by which the state of moving through the sky and the state of Śiva are indeed attained within one's own body. RCint_1.19
"You are the mother of all beings, and I am the eternal father;
O Goddess, that which is the essence of the two, born from the great union," RCint_1.20 //
O beloved, through seeing it, touching it, eating it,
dying [with it], worshipping it, and offering it as a liquid, a sixfold fruit is observed.
Whatever merit is gained from seeing the Kedāra and other such lingas on earth,
that same merit is obtained from the sight of the mercury.
The essence contained within sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, when blended together, is the worship of Śiva for the sake of attaining his presence. RCint_1.23 //
O Supreme Goddess, by consuming this elixir, one destroys the threefold suffering;
that supreme state, difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, is thereby reached.
O Supreme Goddess, by remembering the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) situated within the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one is instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over many lifetimes.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the perfect worship of a thousand self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅgas,
that fruit shall be multiplied ten millionfold by the worship of a mercury-liṅga (rasaliṅga).
He who gives medicinal juice, prepared with purification and proper cooking, to the sick,
obtains the eternal fruit of the Tulā-dāna and the Aśvamedha sacrifices.
The science of alchemy is the supreme knowledge, difficult to obtain even throughout the three worlds;
since it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, it should be known as endowed with all virtues.
Even if that sinner who reviles the Veda were endowed with the knowledge of Brahman,
I would not be his protector even in hundreds of millions of births.
Whoever engages in conversation or physical contact with those who revile the tongue shall be tormented by sin for as many as thousands of births.
Gold-digested ash-mercury, when consumed, bestows the state of Rudra;
silver-digested mercury bestows the state of Viṣṇu, while that digested by the sun (copper) bestows the state of Brahmā.
Through *tīkṣṇa* one attains the state of a lord of wealth; through *jīrṇa*, the state of the Sun;
through *tālaka*, the state of the Moon; and through *rohaṇa*, kingship and immortality.
But by means of the general sharp [mantra], a man may attain the state of Śakra.
When devoid of defects, the rasa is Brahmā; when swooned, it is Janārdana;
when killed, it takes the form of Rudra; and when bound, it is Sadāśiva himself.
Even the Lotus-born Brahmā himself would not be able to reach the end of such qualities even with words lasting for great eons; therefore, enough of this prolixity.
Whatever work of the Lord of Sūtas was performed by me, or which it was possible for me to cause others to perform, has been set forth here.
Those who teach this but do not cause it to be performed, and those who perform it but do not study it—both of these have false purposes.
Now, we shall explain the chapter on *mūrcchanās*.
(mūrcchanā:
[medical] definition) Mūrcchanā is the state of being an unfailing destroyer of disease. RCint_2.2 //

Following the worship and recollection of the respective deities as prescribed in their specific tantras, those of subtle intellect— observing the gradations among the various mercury-essences (*rasendra*) that have been thoroughly purified through numerous processes of refinement according to the analogy of fire produced from grass, a flint, or a gem— should perform the purification of mercury even with half a *pala*, and indeed even with a measure of two *vyāvahārika-tolaka*s, in accordance with the statement of the *Rasārṇava*: "The purification of mercury must be performed [even with such small amounts]."
The purified essence is to be made into a paste.
Furthermore, the types of *mūrcchanās* are manifold.

Without the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury by means of the qualities and potencies of the *rasas*, this sovereign mercury (*rasendra*) is indeed incapable of removing disease; it is well known that it does not attain the status of an elixir (*rasāyana*) unless it has undergone the heating (*pāka*) of mercury and silver. (RCint 2.5)
The two types of sand-machines (*sikatā-yantra*) are said to be caused by that [sand-machine]. // RCint_2.6 //

Just as one would take a very hard glass jar smeared with clay, sky-cloth (*mṛd-ambara*), and so forth, which has been thoroughly compressed without limit, and which contains a medicinal essence (*rasagarbhin*) of the type to be described later; having placed it upon a suitable vessel that has a hole the size of a forefinger below, and having first packed salt around it to the extent of two or three finger-breadths to leave no gaps, one then fills it with sand up to the neck.
The *vardhamānaka* [crucible] should be filled and heated by the flame of fire for three, four, five, or six days in succession; this is one type of apparatus.
(Vālukāyantra): A clay vessel,

about one cubit in measurement, buried within the earth, with its mouth neither too flattened nor too high, resembling an ink-pot, and having the opening of its mouth closed by either a circular rim of earthenware or a circular rim of glass, as described previously.
Alternatively, having prepared a crucible with dried cow-dung cakes, a seal should be placed on top; this is another apparatus.
Trilocana states that [the process of] jāraṇa is performed using a metal crucible consisting of two unequal fragments, either within a *sikatāyantra* or in a *bhūdharayantra*.
"In the *kūrmayantra*, the wise one should cause mercury to digest six times its weight of sulfur"—thus say others. (Mercury:: *jāraṇa*) RCint_2.10.

In this case, the dyeing would not occur in that manner; therefore, having first caused the five qualities to undergo digestion (*jāraṇa*), the remaining single [quality] should be digested in a small vessel (*kūpikā*) and so forth, whereby the dyeing will be successful.
In this context, they digest even pure sulfur through habituation, without the use of kajjali.

Having recognized the pervasive mercury— which has entered the hollow of the crucible, possesses the qualities of mercury, and is balanced with sulphur— by means of the process of heating, one should slowly cook it in a *sikatāyantra* (sand-bath apparatus).
By this fire-ritual, one should repeatedly effect the exhaustion of the sulphur until it attains the luster of vermilion; having experienced this, I have described this sequence of practice.
Even without *āroṭaka*, *rasasindūra* can be produced from a paste made of *hiṅgula* and sulfur. (RCint 2.14)
Having prepared a paste (*piṣṭī*) here consisting of three parts of mercury and one part each of gold, mica, silver, and lotus,
and having rendered it into a paste by means of the juices, qualities, and strength [of the ingredients], mix it continuously with the waters of the *kumārī* plant. (RCint 2.15)
This [mercury] should be joined with six times [the amount of] sulfur by means of the digestion through the power of the "upward-and-downward" (*adharottara*) samādhi.
In the yoga [process], the paste (*piṣṭi*) is to be cooked for the purpose of producing *kajjalī* and for the purpose of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
This method is accomplished by means of a downward-acting apparatus alone, and not by an upward-acting one.
A jar may be made of glass or clay; sometimes it is made of gold, iron, or silver.
(Regarding the approximate coating of the jar:)
A plaster made from lime mixed with an abundance of chalk and salt has been prepared.

By means of these two instruments, the wise cause even abundant gold, mercury, and metallic essences to be digested; let them further cause [these matters] to sprout anew through their own clear and excellent investigations as they desire. RCint_2.19.
The mercury, colored by the hundredfold fragrance of the inner-smoke (*antardhūma*) processed [by heating], is thus dyed.
That [mercury] becomes a "thousand-piercer" (sahasravedhī) when applied to silver, copper, and tin.
Having placed a quantity of mercury equal to the amount of lead in a small earthen vessel called a *sikatāyantra*,
one should place the mercury therein with a specific type of oil, observing it once more until half its body is submerged. (RCint 2.21)
One should add sulfur six times in very small quantities until it is digested; thus, the mercury becomes powerful.
When employed in all mercurial preparations, this undoubtedly destroys disease with speed.
In this context, they employ substances such as snake-venom and mercury in debates and in yogic practices for the purpose of producing a "piṣṭi" (a ground or composite preparation).

The milk of *snuhī* and *arka*, seeds of *brahma*, *guggulu*, and double the amount of rock salt (*saindhava*) should be rubbed together; this is the most excellent "shackle" (*nigaḍa*) for mercury. (RCint 2.24)

If mercury— mixed with *rasasindūra*, *nigaḍa*, *māraka*, water, and white rock salt— is placed inside a small crucible (*kūpikā*) upon sand and heated repeatedly in this manner, then this king of mercury attains a firm bond (*bandha*).
Having filled a well-constructed crucible halfway with one-fourth part of salt,
one should place a fourth part of mercury upon it along with the dust of red bricks.
Having placed white rock salt in a crystal vessel of equal size upon it,
one should grind together pure rock salt and pure mercury with water from a virgin girl, using a crystal pestle.
Having prepared the appropriate *parpaṭa* and placed it upon that [vessel] in the same manner, one should then add rock salt and *saindhava* salt; from this, the mercury (*rasa*) will flow out.
For the sake of obtaining [the desired result], one should place shards of broken pottery over that, cover it with another sturdy vessel,
seal it, and cook it according to the ritual procedure for three days.
Here, the elders prescribe bhallātaka, even though it was not mentioned, as being equal to mercury.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on bondage (bandhana).
Bondage consists in being bound by a material form (mūrti), characterized by natural fluidity that is not destroyed by fire.
Even this ghee, oil, and so forth, perfected through the ripening of forest herbs, possesses irresistible potency;
how much more so this one, born from the body of the Lord, who has been matured by the dense radiance of Jambunada gold and the moon?
(19) There are nineteen rites that accomplish these [processes]:

crushing (*mardana*), softening (*mūrchana*), raising (*utthāpana*), sweating (*svedana*), casting down (*pātana*), awakening (*bodhana*), restraining (*niyamana*), inflaming (*saṃdīpana*), fumigation (*anuvāsana*), the measure of the swallowing of the ether and so forth (*gaganādi-grāsa-pramāṇa*), moving (*cāraṇa*), internal liquefaction (*garbha-druti*), external liquefaction (*bāhya-druti*), alchemical digestion through yoga (*yoga-jāraṇa*), coloring (*rañjana*), extraction of essence (*sāraṇa*), transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), piercing (*vedhana*), and consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*).

(Religious rites prior to commencing the *saṃskāras*): Having worshipped the venerable Guru, the maiden, the *baṭuka*, the Lord of Ganas, the Yoginīs, and the Kṣetrapālas, preceded by the fourfold offering (*caturdhābali*).
At an auspicious moment, during the strength of the moon,
one should extract the mercury into a very firm mortar made of stone or iron, produced from the essence [of minerals].
Having placed it upon a smooth, clear four-finger-thick cushion,
it should be protected by two or three attendants who have mastered the mantras.
The physician should rub the mercury with the combined powders in a sixteenfold proportion,
using cloth-strained liquids and other substances to be described hereafter.
One should rub and cause the mercury (sūta) to faint, then revive it seven times with red brick,
turmeric, soot-essence, wool-ash, and tumbī.
Combined with the juice of the jambīra fruit, for the removal of the defects of the nāgas.
One releases the defect of mercury by means of the powder of *viśālāṅkola*,
together with the powder of the root of *rājavṛkṣa* and *kanyā*.
For the purpose of removing the defects of impurity,
the auspicious rubbing and raising [of the mercury] should be performed with the juices of black dhattūra to eliminate its volatility.
For the pacification of the defects of poison, one should use the water of Triphalā and Kanyakā;
for the defect of the mountain (giri-doṣa), one should diligently use Trikaṭu with the water of Kanyakā.
The destruction of fire [impurity] occurs through the powder of *citraka* along with *kanyā*;
one should purify it according to each specific humor (*doṣa*) using warm *āranāla*.
Thus purified, the mercury (*sūta*) is freed from the seven defects.
For he becomes a performer of his duty, whereas otherwise he would be a destroyer of his duty.
The physician should collect the mercury adhering to the upper vessel by placing the powder remaining from the *utthāpana* process into a *pātana* apparatus. (RCint 3.13)
Having tied the liquid extract in a cloth four times its size, one should cook it by the dolā method for one day in a decoction of *vyoṣa*, *varā*, *vahni*, and *kanyā*, along with *kāñjika*.
This sudation is prescribed for the purpose of eliminating the remainder of the humors.
One should fill an earthen vessel with various grains as they are available, provided they are husked and mixed with water; one should keep it protected until it reaches acidity. RCint_3.15.
In the midst of that are ghanavāṅmuṇḍī, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā,
mīnākṣī, sarpākṣī, sahadevī, and śatāvarī.
One should grind triphalā, girikarṇī, haṃsapādī, and citraka, together with their roots and stalks, and add them according to availability. RCint_3.17 //
This *dhānyāmlaka* (gruel-water) is produced within a vessel that has previously held sour liquids;
one should employ it everywhere for the sudation and other processes of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*).
Or one should employ *amlamāranāla* in its absence.
(For *ūrdhvapātana*:
three parts of mercury and one part of iron powder [arke-cūrṇa], then with *nimbuka* fruits...)
One should knead this until it attains the state of a solid mass.
One should place that lump of clay, which was held in a vessel at the bottom, into a vessel above;
having prepared a basin, someone should provide it with a moist cloth.
Having sealed the fire beneath it, one should awaken the fourfold restraint;
then, by means of the proper technique, one should take the mercury adhering to the upper vessel.
This is called "upward sublimation" (*ūrdhvapātana*) by physicians in the purification of mercury;
[it serves] to block the joints (*sandhirodha*).
One should swallow another vessel whose mouth contains the medicinal paste;
likewise, a joint should be made between the two in the three-fold *pātanā* apparatus.
The dimensions and measurements of the yantra should be learned from the mouth of the guru by those who are discerning.
Because there is no fixed measure for aesthetic flavor (rasa), it cannot be described at all.

Having ground for a day with jambu-juice the mercury known as *navanīta*, one should treat it with *vānarī*, *śigru*, and *śikhin*, combined with salt and *asurī*. (This is the process of *adhaḥpātana*.)
Knowing the mercury to have become "destroyed and powdered" (naṣṭapiṣṭa), one should smear it inside an upper vessel;
having smeared the interior of the upper vessel, its lower part should be filled with water.
Having applied a cementing seal at the joint of the two [vessels], one should fill that apparatus with earth;
when a lid is placed on top, the mercury falls into the water.
The process called "downward precipitation" (*adhaḥpātana*) has been described by the Siddhas and others for the ritual of extraction (*sūtaka*).
Having poured the mercury into a jar, one should place another jar containing water [over it]. (This is *tiryakpātana*.)
Having turned the faces of the two [channels] sideways, the wise one should block their openings.
One should ignite the fire beneath the mercury until the mercury enters the water;
this is called *tiryakpātana* (horizontal sublimation) by the perfected masters such as Nāgārjuna and others.
If lead (nāga) and tin (vaṅga) have been mixed into the mercury for the sake of sale,
an artificial defect will arise from them; its removal occurs through three sublimations (pātana).
In this way, mercury reduced to a state of calcination attains a state of impotence;
for its liberation, "awakening" (bodhana) is performed, and that is now described. (RCint 3.30)
Either in a skull of Viśvāmitra, or in a glass jar,
one should place a lotus born of creation and remain there until it has completely dissolved.
One should fill it with earth for three days to the measure of a *rājahasta*;
by this, this king of mercury abandons its impotent state.
Having covered the liquid inside the vessel with salt and sour flour (*lavaṇāmlapiṣṭa*),
and having added a little sour water, one should seal it with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*). (RCint 3.33)
A light seal should be applied from above so that the mercury regains its breath;
otherwise, through such torment, this mercury will subsequently become impotent.
And for the intensification of vigor, one should apply fomentation to a birch-bark leaf soaked in water containing powdered rock salt.
By means of *sarpākṣī*, *ciñcikā*, *vandhyā*, *bhṛṅga*, *abdaka*, and *kanakāmbu*, the mercury,
having been subjected to sweating for a day, attains stability through this restrictive process (*niyamana*). (RCint 3.35)
(dīpana) Green vitriol, the five salts, black mustard seeds, black pepper, two kinds of śigru seeds, and borax— all combined together. RCint_3.36.
Having stirred it in sour gruel (kāñjika) and cooked it in a dolāyantra for three days,
the digestive fire (dīpana) of the king of mercury (sūtarāja) becomes properly activated for the process of assimilation (jāraṇa).
Alternatively, one should cook it in *kāñjika* with the juices of *citraka* for three days; thus,
an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) is produced for that king of mercury.
The king of essences (rasarāja), ignited by *anuvāsana* and combined with the juice of *jambīra*,
should be kept for one day in the heat within an earthen vessel or one made of stone.
Regarding the definition of *jāraṇā*:

*Jāraṇā* indeed consists in the state of having attained a prior condition preceded by the swallowing (*grāsa*) of dense gold and other substances, distinct from the processes of falling (*pātana*) and straining (*gālana*). (RCint 3.40)

Furthermore, it has been stated that only those embodied beings who have made their bodies into fields for the digestion of solid gold and the like possess the qualification for consumption. RCint_3.41 //
And its fruit has been stated by the Lord himself:
"When the destruction of all sins has occurred, the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇā*) is attained."
Upon its attainment, the very cognition characterized by liberation would indeed be attained.
O Goddess, for the practitioner, *jāraṇa* (digestion) is that which manifests liberation;
the mortar is the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), O Goddess, and the mercury-king is said to be the linga.
Massaging, saluting, and even the taking of morsels are prescribed as forms of worship for as many days as the mercury remains within the fire during the process of digestion (jāraṇa).
He who offers a fire-oblation for even a single day to the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) is glorified in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of years.
His sins dissolve away, and even while performing them, he is not defiled.
Just as those who do not smelt the scent of iron and gold seek a noble result from mercury,
so too are those farmers and physicians dull-witted who expect a harvest from an unplowed field.
When an equal amount of sulphur has been digested, the mercury becomes a hundred times purer;
when twice the amount of sulphur has been digested, it is the supreme remedy for all types of leprosy.
When three parts of sulfur have been digested [by the mercury], it destroys all dullness;
when four parts have been digested therein, it destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
"When the five-fold mercury is digested by sulphur, it brings about the destruction of [all] decay;
when the six-fold mercury is digested by sulphur, it removes all diseases.
Śrī Bhairava himself spoke this to the Goddess with certainty. (RCint 3.49)
In the process of *jāraṇa* (digestion), a ball should be formed there with the paste of sulfur (*gandha*) for the digestion of sulfur.
Therefore, when a sattva of space (vyoma) equal to that has been digested, it is a hundred times more effective;
indeed, when a sattva of mica, borax, or mercury and so forth has been digested, it brings about excellent qualities.
When mercury has been processed with gold, it bestows a thousandfold collection of qualities;
as for the qualities of mercury processed with diamonds and other minerals, Śiva alone knows them.
The menstrual blood of the Goddess becomes the scent, and her seminal element likewise becomes mica;
both become capable of embracing due to their fondness for the semen of Śiva.
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the supreme state is attained;
just as there may be much digestion (jāraṇā), so too may the mercury possess many qualities (guṇa).
(Regarding Mercury as one seeking to devour:
One should pierce a vajra-thorn with a vajra-point eight finger-breadths long using clay;
having smeared it with cow dung and roasted it in a small fire, it should then be dried there.
Thrown into the hollow of the thunderbolt for three days, the mercury becomes hungry;
it instantly devours scent, gold, and so forth, as well as Vajrasattva and the rest.
(Regarding Mercury as the *grāsārthin*):

Another method is that mercury, having become digested through the sixfold strength described in the chapter on *mūrchā*, and having emerged from the paste (*piṣṭikā*) in the mortar (*khalva*), being extremely hungry, quickly devours thick gold, diamond, metallic essences (*sattva*), and so forth.
Others practice by performing both of these two procedures. RCint_3.57.
Mercury, seeking to be devoured, when soaked for three days in a mixture of alum, borax, *svarji*, sal-ammoniac, and copper,
and then infused with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), causes mercury, sulphur, and other substances to flow out instantly.
When mercury is thrown into feces mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika), it becomes eager for a morsel;
it devours all metals, and like a thunderbolt (vajra), it devours all living beings.
One should macerate conch powder with the milky sap of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*) in the sunlight for one day;
likewise, one should macerate *dhūmasāra* with the juice of raw *jambīra* fruit for one day.
Sauvarcala salt should be infused with goat’s urine for four watches;
and kantakarī should be boiled for one day in human urine.
Svarjikṣāra, tintiḍīka, kāsīsa,
and śilājatu should be processed separately with juices extracted from jambīra fruits for four watches (yāmas) each.
One should soak dehusked *jayapāla* seeds with the juices of radishes for one day,
and *saindhava*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *guñjā* with the water of *śigru* roots for one day.
All of this should be ground together in equal parts with the juice of fresh jambīra fruits;
one should carefully preserve that pill—this is the *viḍa* known as *vaḍavānala*.
The mercury, processed with this and placed in a heated mortar,
instantly devours all metals such as gold and their essential ores.
The alkali of radish, fresh ginger, and saltpeter, filtered through cow's urine.
The liquid, strained through cloth, should be taken; with it, one should saturate the sulphur a hundred times in a hot, dry place. This is *viḍa* salt, used for the digestion of gold.
[The preparation of] *viḍa* [salt]: with the alkalis of radish, fresh ginger, and *citraka*, strained through cow urine.

(Lead::
Killing) Having placed lead in a crucible, one should add powdered realgar; when it has melted, it is encapsulated with mercury and the liquid of *nimbu* (citron), and it quickly turns to ash.

Likewise, crooked [mercury] should be powdered and mixed with *tālaka* (mica); it should be fired with *gandhāmla* (sulphuric acid) until it is free from all defects, at which point it may be employed in medicinal formulations.

Having ground together a serpent from the earth (*bhūbhujaṅgama*) and *agasti*, one should smear the vessel; therein, when the mercury (*nāga*) has been liquefied with vitriol (*vidruta*), one should add [the juice] derived from *vāsā* and *apāmārga*.
One should mix alkaline salt there in a fourth part according to the teacher’s instruction;
one should cook it on the hearth for one prahara, stirring with a ladle made of vāsā wood.
Then, having extracted that powder, one should grind it with the juice of *vāsā*.
Having extracted it again, one should roast it (*puṭayet*) and grind it with that same liquid.
In this manner, after seven roastings, the lead (*nāga*) will certainly become vermilion (*sindūra*).

(Regarding the killing of iron: One should repeatedly throw red-hot iron leaves into a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) until they are reduced to powder; then one should cook them again in a decoction of *triphalā* mixed with cow’s urine.

One should then perform *puṭapāka* (sealed heating) using *matsyākṣī* and *triphalā* until the iron becomes "un-arisen" (*niruttha*). Afterwards, having been well-sealed and saturated with clarified butter and honey, the iron is perfected.
In this context, *matsyāk�pī* means *machchhī*.
One should add a small amount of realgar (*manaḥśilā*) to the three or four layers under discussion. (RCint 6.56)

Iron filings soaked in pomegranate leaves should be placed in a small shallow vessel and covered with cloth; it is killed by the rays of the sun. It should then be subjected to *puṭapāka* treatments using *triphalā* and other such ingredients.

For the sake of increasing the quality, one should apply multiple layers (puṭas), such as a hundred or more; having made it resemble a mung bean, one should apply the layers and not filter it with cloth.
The *triphalā* and other formulations will be described in the *Amṛtasāraloha*.
Having given twice the amount of mercury (*sūtaka*) of sulphur (*gandha*), one should prepare a collyrium (*kajjalī*).
One should grind equal amounts of iron powder with the juice of kanyākā.
Then, having formed a pill from the pair of *yāmā* [ingredients] in a copper vessel,
the wise one should place it in the sun and cover it with *urvūka* leaves.
Heat should be applied for half a watch (yāma), after which one should place it upon a heap of grain;
having placed a shallow bowl on top, one should remove it at the end of three days.
Having ground it, one should strain it through cloth; in this way, it becomes water-soluble.
In the same manner, one should "kill" all metals, including gold and the others as well.
(Regarding iron: testing the *vāritara* state) All this dead iron should be smelted with the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*).
If it should thus become non-recurrent (*nirutthāna*), then indeed that is to be known as *vāritara*. RCint_6.63 //
Honey, clarified butter, *guñjā*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and likewise *guggulu*— this is the "fivefold friend" (*mitrapañcaka*), reckoned for the purpose of melting metals.
One should place honey, clarified butter, dead iron, and silver together within a sealed crucible.
When it has been sealed and blown [into a furnace], one should collect the silver according to its previous weight;
then one should know the iron to be "dead" (consumed), otherwise one should cause it to die again.
One should grind iron that has been raised by means of sulphur in an equal amount within a mortar.
Having sealed [the substance] for one day with the juices of *kanyākā*, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
in this very manner, this process of *nirutthiti* (reversal of dissolution) should be performed for all metals.
Gold should be employed by increasing it by a barley-corn (*yava*) at each step, starting from eight *guñjās* for the sun;
silver is double that amount, while other metals are increased by three times that.
Regarding the quality of the rust (*kiṭṭa*): that which is over a hundred years old is the best, while that which is eighty years old is middling.
The lowest [type] is sixty years old; it is even worse than poison.

One should blow upon the dross produced from iron using charcoal from *akṣa* wood; then, one should sprinkle it with cow's urine each time it has been heated again and again, repeating this process seven times.

Then, having ground it into powder and stirred it with double the amount of decoctions derived from the three myrobalans (triphalā), one should roast it over a fire; thus, excellent maṇḍūra is produced.
(Gold and silver) are meritorious, bestowing longevity, prosperity, splendor, wisdom, and memory; they destroy all diseases,
pacify possession by malevolent spirits, grant the bliss of love, and illuminate happiness and nourishment.
Furthermore, silver from the Ganges, when ground into a paste, prevents aging, removes urinary disorders,
clearly brings nourishment to those who are emaciated, and is the cause for the increase of virility.
Gold is sweet and pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and its potency (*vīrya*) is cooling;
it pacifies all the *doṣas*, destroys poison, and eliminates *garas*. (RCint 6.72)
The practice of this [mantra] is the destroyer of misfortune, strife, and sin;
it bestows long life, intelligence, and memory, and increases nourishment and splendor.
Those diseases which have not been overcome by the application of all medicinal herbs,
even by means of the five types of ritual actions (*karma*), upon those one should employ gold.
Through the application of bitumen (śilājatu), as well as that of copper and mercury,
and by other elixirs (rasāyana) as well, the application of gold is supreme.
In the phrase "of the heated [metal] and the mercury" (tāpyasūtakayoḥ), it should be understood that the mercury is one that has undergone general purification;
for mercury that has undergone specific purification bestows such qualities as the power of traveling through the sky.
Having consumed this triad of honey, *āmalaka* powder, and gold,
even one seized by an *ariṣṭa* (fatal omen) is liberated from the danger to life.
One desiring intelligence should use *vacā*; one desiring prosperity, lotus filaments;
one seeking long life, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*; and one desiring progeny, *vidārī*.
Copper, known by the name of the Sun, cures abdominal tumors, anemia, chronic digestive disorders, and colic; it scrapes the impurities from the heart, destroys worms, and acts as a purifier.
It alleviates splenic disorders, skin diseases, abdominal enlargement, and peptic ulcers, and it removes phlegm and wind. (RCint 6.79)
Bell-metal (pittala) and brass (kāṃsya) destroy phlegm and bile; brass is heating and scraping.
Tin (vaṅga) removes burning sensations and destroys anemia, worms, and urinary disorders.
Dead lead possesses the strength of ten elephants; it increases virility, longevity, and luster, and destroys diseases. Mercury (raṅga) also possesses these same qualities when processed.
It conquers thirst, swelling, colic, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, anemia, and urinary disorders;
it is age-defying, heavy, beneficial for the eyes, laxative, and removes fat and wind.
Lead (nāga) is a color-enhancer for silver and removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
Iron bestows longevity, generates strength and virility, removes diseases, and acts as a destroyer of fatigue;
indeed, there is nothing equal to iron as the most excellent elixir (*rasāyana*) for human beings. (RCint 6.84)
The *krauñca* is twice as effective as the *sāmānya*; the *kaliṅga* is eight times more than that;
the *bhadra* is ten times more than the *kali*; and the *vajra* is a thousand times more effective than the *bhadra*.
Diamond is a hundred times stronger than steel; lead is ten times stronger than that;
and from that, magnetite is a thousand times stronger and possesses great power.
Whatever metal is described as having certain qualities, its dross (kiṭṭa) possesses those same qualities as well.
Now, we shall expound the chapter on the preparation of poisons and metallic salts.
For that which is called poison, being the most potent of all elixirs, attains the capacity to destroy every disease.

That [poison] indeed consists of eighteen varieties, wherein the following types must be collected for the purpose of application: *saktuka*, *mustaka*, *kaurma*, *dārvīka*, *sārṣapa*, *saikata*, *vatsanābha*, and *śvetaśṛṅgin*.
When well-grounded, it resembles a variegated lotus root;
one should know that to be *saktuka*, which possesses a long-lasting impulse and is extremely intense.
Mustaka has a short stalk, destroys diseases, resembles musta in shape,
and originates from Kaurma and Dārvīka.
The tortoise-shaped [vessel] is for the Kaurma [rite], and the one shaped like the hood of a snake is for the Dārvīka.
The *sārṣapa* [fever] removes fever; it is covered with mustard seeds and *kaṇā* [grains],
joined with large and small white and yellow spots, and is devoid of body hair.
The bulb known as *saikata* is said to destroy all diseases, such as fever and others.
The *vatsanābha* is a bulb shaped like a cow’s udder; it is not longer than five finger-breadths, nor is it thicker than a cow’s udder. This *vatsanābhaka* is of two kinds.
It acts quickly, is easily abandoned, and may be white or black; otherwise, it becomes different. It should be employed for the removal of diseases, for the process of *jāraṇā*, and for *rasāyana*.
(Śvetaśṛṅgī):
Śṛṅgī is like a cow’s horn, being white both on the outside and inside.

These preparations, such as *saktuka* and others, should be administered in cases of wind disorders (*vāta*) and the like, as well as in cases of insanity (*unmāda*) and the combined derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), when there is a conjunction with blood.
The ten types of poison—namely *kālakūṭa*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *dardura*, *hālāhala*, *karkoṭa*, *granthi*, *hāridra*, *raktaśṛṅgī*, *kesara*, and *yamadaṃṣṭrā*—should be avoided. RCint_7.12 //
That bulbous root which is round, black, and resembles a jambīra fruit—
one should know that as kālakūṭa, which brings death by mere inhalation. (RCint 7.13)
*Meṣaśṛṅgī*:
A bulbous root shaped like a ram's horn is known as *meṣaśṛṅgī*.
(*Dardura*)
The bulbous root that has the appearance of a frog is called *dardura*.
One should recognize Halāhala as being blue within and white without;
[and] Karkoṭa.
The *karkoṭa* resembles the *karkoṭa* flower; it is harsh on the outside and soft within.
The *hāridra* [variety] has a knot like that of turmeric; it is black in color and extremely terrifying.
It should be well-rounded at both the base and the tip, elongated, and have a yellow interior.
The bulbous root (kandaka) should be richly covered with scales, have smooth joints, and be turmeric-colored.
When the tip of a cow's horn is slightly incised, blood flows out; that which has a bulbous root like a cow's udder is called *raktaśṛṅgī*, and its poison is [to be treated] as follows. RCint_7.17.
That filament which has a white luster within the interior is known as *kesara*;
(*yamadaṃṣṭrā*).
Having the form and configuration of a dog's fang, she is called Yamadaṃṣṭrā.
These ten [substances] are employed in alchemy of mercury, alchemy of metals, and occasionally in alchemy of poisons; they are not used in medicinal elixirs (*rasāyana*).
One should harvest it at the time of fruit ripening; it should be fresh, unctuous, dense, heavy, unblemished, and not withered by wind or other factors that counteract poisons.
Having made portions of the poison as large as chickpeas and placed them in a vessel,
one should pour cow's urine over them every day, using fresh urine each time.
Then, having held it in intense sunlight for more than three days, one should dry it; thereafter, one should employ that poison in medicinal applications according to the prescribed dosage.
One should carefully store pure poison on a cloth smeared with red mustard oil;
otherwise, its potency will be lost.
That poison, when ground together with borax, is said to be "dead";
one should employ it in all diseases, for it does not cause any adverse reaction.
Poison is of four types according to its color and caste: white, red, yellow, and black.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra are to be known in that order.
A Brahmin who removes all diseases becomes a Kṣatriya, and one who practices alchemy becomes a Vaiśya; even a Śūdra may become a healer of diseases, but he is censured everywhere.
A Brāhmaṇa is given [as a fee] in cases of disease; a Kṣatriya in the case of consuming poison;
a Vaiśya in all types of illnesses; and a Śūdra in the case of being bitten by a snake.
One should not administer it during autumn, summer, spring, or the rainy season;
however, if administered for four months, it removes diseases such as leprosy and skin eruptions.
As long as one practices [the consumption of] poison starting from eight barley grains down to the size of a sesame seed,
it will pacify all diseases and bring about the nourishment of the gaze.
On the first day, the dose is one mustard seed; on the second, two mustard seeds;
and likewise on the third, fourth, and fifth days.
In the sixth and seventh [stages], one should increase it by gradual increments;
one should lead through the first group of seven with the measure of seven mustard seeds.
In the same manner, the poison should be administered in decreasing doses during the second week;
in the third week, a dose of the size of a barley grain should be given progressively.

It should be administered according to the increase or decrease [of the patient's strength]; likewise, on the fourth and seventh days, one who is healthy should swallow a dose the size of a barley grain (*yava*), while one suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) should swallow a dose the size of a *guñjā* berry.
Poison should not be administered to one who is eighty years of age, nor to one who is eighty years old; indeed, if given to such a person, it will cause harm.
It should be administered in all diseases to one who eats ghee and wholesome food;
it should be applied to a man who consumes milk and is devoted to the practice of *rasāyana*.
One should practice that which is like poison while maintaining celibacy as the primary principle;
by remaining well-composed through wholesome means, success will then follow without a doubt.
When a mortal, through negligence, consumes poison in an excessive dose, then eight stages (vegas) arise for that embodied being. (Poison: 8 stages) RCint_7.37.
In the first stage there is intense heat; in the second, trembling occurs;
in the third stage there is a burning sensation; and in the fourth, one falls to the ground.
In the fifth impulse, there is froth; in the sixth, there is impairment;
in the seventh impulse, there is numbness; and in the eighth, death occurs.
Having recognized these as the onsets of poison, one should destroy them by means of mantras and tantras. RCint_7.40 //
When food has been eaten in excessive measure, one should then induce vomiting.
One should administer goat’s milk until vomiting occurs;
when the goat’s milk has become stabilized within the patient's digestive tract,
the skilled physician should know that the force of the poison has been overcome.
A decoction of *rajanī* and *meghanāda*, when drunk, destroys poison;
likewise, *sarpākṣī* or borax taken with clarified butter is a supreme remover of poison.
Or, the marrow of *putrajīvaka* drunk with lime juice (*nimbuka*) water certainly destroys the force of poison,
just as rain extinguishes a forest fire.

Poison should not be administered to one who is angry, nor to one afflicted by bile, nor to a eunuch, nor to one suffering from pulmonary consumption; nor to one engaged in hunger, thirst, fatigue, heat, or travel, nor to one with wasting disease;
nor among pregnant women, children, or the elderly, nor within the royal palace.
Poison should never be given or consumed during a debate;
however, it may be consumed by the teacher as a means to inspire confidence in the disciple.
The subtypes of poison are: kālakūṭa, vatsanābha, śṛṅgika, pradīpana,
hālāhala, brahmaputra, hāridra, and likewise saktuka.
These nine varieties of poison are said to be: the *saurāṣṭrika*. RCint_7.47 //
(Upaviṣa):
Arka, sehuṇḍa, dhustūra, lāṅgalī, karavīraka, guñjā, and ahiphena—these are the seven species of upaviṣa. RCint 7.48.
Mercury, when rubbed with these [substances], becomes "severed of its wings" (*chinnapakṣa*) due to the poison.
And his mouth becomes extremely voracious for devouring the bodily elements.
White, red, yellow, and black are the Vajra lineages of the twice-born and so forth;
one should identify them by their characteristics as being female, male, or neuter in nature.
Those which are circular, complete with ridges, radiant, and very large, are declared to be male vajras,
being devoid of lines and dots.
Those hexagons, joined with lines and points, are considered to be the female vajras.
Those which are triangular, broad, and long are to be known as neuter (*napuṃsaka*). (Vajra :: Neuter) RCint_7.53 //
Among all [substances], males are the best for piercing (*vedhana*) and binding mercury (*rasabandha*).
The female *vajra* is for the sake of attaining the perfection of the body (*dehasiddhi*), while the neuter (*napuṃsaka*) is used for transmutation (*krāmaṇa*).
The Brahmin is said to be [the master] in alchemy (rasāyana), the Kṣatriya in the destruction of diseases;
one should know the Vaiśya in debate, and the fourth [the Śūdra] in the arresting of old age.
A female [mantra] should be given to women, and likewise a neuter one to eunuchs;
however, among all [these], those that are masculine and most powerful should always be employed.

Having cast [the vajra] into the interior of a tigress-root bulb and subjected it to seven *puṭa* cycles, it becomes purified by quenching it with horse urine at each cycle. (Vajra-purification) RCint_7.57.
(Vajra:: Māraṇam) Having ground the root of either a three-year-old *nāgavallī* or *kārpāsī*,
one should place the *vajra* within it and seal the crucible.
Indeed, one dies without deliberation by means of elephant-bulb preparations in the measure of human beings.
The wise one, having seized a frog and placed it in a vessel made of bell-metal, should keep it there;
terrified, it will urinate therein, and into that urine one should cast the *vajra*.
If heated again and again in many ways, even a diamond would thus meet its destruction.
One should repeatedly heat the vajra and immerse it twenty-one times in a decoction of horse gram mixed with asafoetida and rock salt; thus it will turn to ash. (Vajra-māraṇa, RCint 7.60)
Wherever there may be mercury in which the *vajra* is present, that mercury is called "immortal" (*amṛta*).
When reduced to ashes through the proper method, it makes the body like a *vajra*.
Vaikrānta, whether blue, white, or red, should be purified in the same manner as the diamond (*vajra*).
Endowed with the characteristics of a diamond, it is incapable of being burned or destroyed.
One should sprinkle that [vaikrānta] with horse urine while it is heated, repeating this twenty-one times;
then, smeared with the five parts of uttaravāruṇī and placed inside a crucible, it is processed by means of *puṭa* applications.
Likewise, vaikrānta (the substitute for vajra) undergoes death when subjected to seven applications of the substance known as kuñjara.
One should employ reduced-to-ashes vaikrānta in place of the diamond (vajra).
(The nine gems:
male-vajra, garuḍodgāra, māṇikya, vāsavopala,
vaidūrya, puṣpa, gomeda, pearl, and coral.
These nine jewels are equal to the essence of nectar.
One should heat gems, pearls, and corals in a dolikāyantra with the fresh juice of jayantī; purification will be achieved in one watch (yāma).
A ruby is purified by sour liquids, a pearl likewise by *jayantī*,
coral by the group of alkaline substances, and emerald by cow’s milk.
One should stabilize a *puṣyarāga* gem with *kulattha* bean decoctions mixed with *taṇḍulīya* water,
and a *vajra* or sapphire (*nīla*) with indigo juice.
One should purify gomedaka with rocanā and vaidūrya with the water of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
According to the scriptures, there would be no fault in using pearls and other such items even if they are impure;
nevertheless, their qualities will increase, especially through purification.

All iron, when cooked with sour substances and alkalis, becomes completely purified; likewise, copper pyrites, realgar, blue vitriol, mica, and orpiment are properly purified. Furthermore, pearls, coral, oyster shells, capala, conch shells, and auspicious cowries become like nectar when cast into milk; and an offering thrown there becomes auspicious. (RCint 7.70)
With *śilā*, *gandhaka*, and *tālaka* ground together with the juice of *lakuca*,
other jewels— excluding diamond (*vajra*)— are indeed killed by means of eight crucibles. RCint_7.71.
One should sprinkle [the gems] with the juice of *taṇḍulīya* and breast milk by a virgin;
each [gem] seven times, until they are all thoroughly heated.
Pearls, corals, and likewise all kinds of gems of various colors perish in an instant; there is no doubt about this.
Just like a vajra, one should likewise purify and slay all jewels. RCint_7.74

(Refining Haritāla) Having bound the *tālaka* in a cloth packet (*poṭṭalī*), one should immerse it in *kāñjika* mixed with powder for one *yāma* using a *dolāyantra*, and then [immerse it] in the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
One should cook it for one watch (yāma) in sesame oil and for one watch in water containing the three myrobalans (triphalā);
having been cooked for four watches in a dolāyantra, the mineral calamine (tālaka) becomes purified.
(Realgar:
purified:
medicinal properties)
Being pure, it bestows beauty and vigor, and acts as a destroyer of death.
(Haritāla: extraction of the essence; precipitation) Lac, turmeric, sesame seeds, drumstick, borax, salt, and jaggery.
Having mixed it with half a *tālaka*, one should seal it in a crucible with a perforated lid;
by firing it in a *pātālayantra* furnace, the essence will certainly fall out.
Haritāla [orpiment]:
For the extraction of its essence,
haritāla mixed with the essence of jaipāla and the seeds of vātārī [is used].
Placed in a vessel within a sand-bath apparatus (*vālukāyantra*), it releases its essence after one watch (*yāma*).
A pill made from roasted *ṭaṅkaṇa* and *tāla*, encased in an iron *parpaṭa*, and blown [into a furnace] by way of the "heavy path" (*gurumārgeṇa*), shall become *indusundarī*. (RCint 7.80)
For the binding of cinnabar,
lac, orpiment, and so forth, an external coating should be applied to the iron leaf with the juice of *bhakta-aṅgāra*.
The essence of realgar (manaḥśilā) should be extracted like that of the palmyra palm (tāla), using those very same medicinal substances.
One should take an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇaka* (borax); when the *tutthaka* (copper sulfate) is smelted, the essence (*sattva*) emerges from it.
Wool, lac, and jaggery, together with borax and gold,
should be ground and carefully made into pills using goat's milk.
When these are blown and heated in a fierce fire, they release their essence as redness.
In this way, the mineral of talaka, śilājatu, vimala, kharpara, and so forth [are used for the extraction of the essence].
They release their own vital essences through the fire of the crucible.

The mineral *khaga* (pyrite), roasted with *śilā* (mica) and *gandhaka* (sulfur), and then ground, [is used for] the precipitation of the essence (*sattvapātana*) and the softening (*mṛdūkaraṇa*) of *kāsīsa*.
Sealed with a copper vessel, it should be smeared and then gently heated.
Having cooked and heated the equal amount of sulphur for four *yāmas*, one should then cook the *tāpya* (borax);
having fried it with half as much sulphur for two *yāmas*, it should be combined with half a *ṭaṅka* of mercury.
When heated in a blind crucible, the essence is released like [impurities from] copper.
For the enhancement of color (the alchemical production of gold), one should cause the following to circulate within a crucible of ash: purified copper, sulfur, and borax.
The pill becomes yellowish in luster, bestowing excellence of complexion.
One should burn seven pieces of *tāpya* (calamine) inside a snake’s clay (*nāgamṛd*);
when blown with fire and treated with *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), it becomes a pill as before. (RCint 7.89)
Having immediately taken *bhūnāga*, the wise one should administer it to a peacock; or else, having made a brave cock enter the house, [he should do the same]. RCint_7.90.

Having taken his feces and urine and discarded the first portion, one should diligently stir them with alkali, honey, and clarified butter, and blow upon them for the sake of sentient beings. RCint_7.91.
By drinking the water from that mudrā, one releases the poison within like a copper vessel;
there is no doubt that both mobile and immobile poisons are destroyed.
Having cooked the *bhūnāgas* with milk, or else with their own earth or with *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
one should form a pellet (*cakrī*) with them after they have been roasted; then, the essence (*sattva*) should be carefully precipitated.
Wherever there is a portion of a secondary metal in the mercury,
the addition of its *sattva* must be performed by one who desires the excellence of that fruit and the mastery of mercury.
(Manaḥśilā:
Purification) Manaḥśilā is purified in a dolāyantra using the juice of jayantī.
For one day, [one should remain] in goat's urine or in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
(Realgar: pure;
medicinal properties)
Śilā is unctuous, pungent, and bitter; it destroys phlegm, is scraping, and is laxative.
Realgar (manaḥśilā),
through its processing in small crucibles and the like, removes the blackness of gold.
Even realgar, campaka, and plantain are liquefied in pungent oil.

(Refining *rasaka*): A crucible (*kharpara*) that has been heated for seven days or even three days in human urine, cow urine, water, or sour gruel, along with rock salt (*saindhava*), becomes purified. RCint 7.98.
(Tuttha:: Purification) One part of mercury, one part of yellow orpiment, four parts of frog, and three parts of *dāraka*— these,
ground with the seeds and heated by the flames of a cuckoo, bind the frog within the house of blindness.
One should grind *tuttha* with an equal amount of *viṣṭhā*, or with an eighth part of *moraṭā*;
having ground it with an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one should then bake it in a small *puṭa*.
Alternatively, *tuttha* becomes pure when baked in honey, especially so.
When vomiting and dizziness no longer exist, then one should declare purification. (Tuttha: Pure: Bodily Reaction) RCint_7.101 //
Tuttha is known to be scraping and breaking; it destroys itching and worms. (RCint 7.102)

(Refining honey: Śigru root well-ground with the expressed juice of Agastya leaves, when enclosed within that [paste], shall be purified; however, tāpya [copper pyrite] is purified by being cooked with sour gruel.
For the purification of honey:
take one part of rock salt (*sindhuja*) and three parts of honey,
[mixing them] with either the juice of *mātuluṅga* or the liquid extracted from *jambīra*.
Having placed it in an iron vessel, one should stir it with an iron ladle;
one should cook it over a gentle fire until it takes on the appearance of vermilion.
One should know this as perfectly purified *mākṣika* and employ it in all diseases.

One should prepare a *sthālīpāka* as previously described using the juices of *gajakarṇa*, *patra*, *mūla*, *śatāvarī*, *bhṛṅga*, and *keśarāja*, either individually or all together. RCint_8.135.

one should afterwards prepare a fine iron powder that resembles mud.
With the juices of triphalā, bhṛṅga, keśara, śatāvarī, kanda, māṇasahaja, bhallātaka, karikarṇacchada root, and punarnavā; RCint_8.138 //

Then, having placed [the substance] in an iron vessel or a clay one— using equal amounts of iron and clay for the two vessels— one should cover the back [of the vessel] and seal the opening at the edge.

the wise one should cover it with abundant wood, dried cow-dung, and husks, and burn it day and night.
In this manner, one should cook [the medicine] by the *puṭapāka* method using these nine kings of herbs—
either with each one individually or with all combined— for three or four times.
For the *puṭapāka* method,
one should grind [the ingredients] after each individual wrapping; having prepared the *sthālīpāka* in that same manner, one should likewise grind it.
One should not grind on such a stone as that upon which fine dust is shed.
If that iron powder, ground and rubbed until smooth on a thick, fine cloth,
should become similar in appearance to the pollen of a *ketakī* flower, then it is excellent.

In the case of a person authorized for the cooking of a sacrificial pot (sthālīpāka), because they have encountered a natural illness, even a medicine that has been prescribed should be rejected, while another suitable medicine should be accepted. (RCint 8.144)

Now we shall describe the process of smelting iron as taught by Nāgārjuna— a process that is imperceptible even to those of intellect as sharp as the tip of a hair or a blade of kuśa grass, who have mastered the ritual procedures for such works.
Regarding the smelting of iron:
having prostrated before Śiva, [one should work] in a strong earthen vessel or a copper cauldron made of iron.

Having poured in the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and the previously mentioned ghee and milk,

If, however, one should see that there is an excess of ghee for the purpose of bathing,

For one whose constitution is characterized by an excess of phlegm (*kapha*), they recommend the consumption of iron in this very manner; for even when eaten alone, this iron produces many virtues. (RCint 8.157)
Alternatively, having taken powdered black soot processed by the prescribed method,
one should take a portion equal to one-fourth, one-half, one, two, three, four, or five times that of the metal.
Having added [the ingredients], one should cook them as before until a powder (rajas) is formed from both;
the quantity of substances such as triphalā should be according to that measure for the *anusmṛti*.
This [milk] is nourishing, it pacifies excessive bile, and it alone generates luster and strength; yet, when administered in an excessively large dose, it greatly suppresses thirst and hunger.
Having made black mica— which is called *bheka*, "the frog," and *vajra*— into single leaves, [one should purify it] until it is moonless (*niścandrika*).
One should grind the powder with a wooden pestle in a wooden mortar.
Furthermore, one should grind the cloth on a stone until it falls through the fine mesh,
and then place it for three days in the abundant juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇikā*.
Then, having extracted that juice, one should carefully grind winter grain porridge with extremely sour, clear water that is free of grit. RCint_8.163.
One should perform the grinding with the fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇikā* itself;
the cooking in a vessel (*sthālīpāka*) and the sealing (*puṭana*) may also be done with the first [group of herbs], such as *bhṛṅgarāja* and others.
Having placed the *piṇḍa* within a leaf of the *arka* plant and so forth, one should set it in the fire of a bellows and burn it for a long time until the fire appears blue.
One should extinguish it by pouring milk over it, or wash it with water;
then, having ground and rubbed it, one should strain it through a cloth to produce a powder free from any specks.
For the pacification of various diseases, for nourishment, and for beauty, one should worship Śiva and,
on a most pure and auspicious day, take that nectar known as *lauha* (iron).
Having again considered the difference in strength and age, [one should determine] that the measure is ten *kṛṣṇalas*;
furthermore, this may be more or even much more, but it is not like a mother’s sweetmeat.
One should grind it again with iron in an iron vessel that is smooth and clean,
adding honey as appropriate, and subsequently add a greater amount of ghee.
Just as one takes hold of a binding by not distinguishing it from the honey,
so too here this [binding] is a visible instrument, while that [result] is invisible through the mantra.
The crushing [of obstacles] occurs with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*; the protection of iron-strength occurs with [the mantra] ending in *phaṭ*;
the offering of food for the iron [deity] occurs with [the mantra] accompanied by *namaḥ*; and [the consumption of it] occurs with [the mantra] ending in *hūm*.

Having consumed that essence of nectar, one should drink either water or milk;
having thoroughly chewed the pure, desire-fulfilling juice, one should drink it, but not swallow it whole.
And having sipped water, if available, one should consume betel-leaf together with camphor.
One should not remain sitting too much, nor speak excessively, nor stand for too long.
One should avoid excessive wind, cold, heat, travel, bathing, and the suppression of natural urges, as well as sleeping during the day and eating at improper times.
One should keep far away from all pungent, sour, bitter, and astringent foods caused by wind or bile,
as well as from sexual intercourse, anger, and fatigue, which are causes for instantaneous destruction.
Let that iron [of hunger] fall later or not; let its sharpness diminish;
let there be pain or no pain in the intestines; let them rumble—food must be eaten without artifice.
Having first drunk milk, one should eat clear, well-prepared,
and non-slimy śāli rice saturated with ghee, generally accompanied by the meat of birds.

The meat of birds that roam the highest saline wastelands, as well as that of goats, antelopes, and the like, is excellent; other meats from aquatic creatures are also superior when compared to those with broad scales.
In the absence of meat, fish that are large and of good quality should be taken as faultless;
the madgura, rohita, and śakula, when roasted, are slightly inferior to fresh flesh.

The fruits of the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *phalaka*, *śeruka*, plantain, palm, coconut, and so forth, as well as other sweet, aphrodisiac fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*) and others, are excellent. (RCint 8.181)
They recommend these— kebuka, tālaka, and karīra, along with the fruits and leaves of vārtāka and paṭola, as well as mudga, masūra, and sugarcane juice— for those who abstain from meat.
All leafy vegetables (śāka) should be avoided; however, one may give vāstuka for the sake of appetite.
One should know that anything other than those prescribed or prohibited stands in the middle category.
Drinking warm milk as an after-drink generally induces purgation in one with a constipated bowel;
likewise, drinking water or the juice of tender coconut fruit serves the same purpose.
If even that does not work, one should drink warm water mixed with alkali;
or warm decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) combined with alkali, which is even more effective than the former.
For three days it should be equal; on the fourth day, however, one should increase it gradually until it reaches eight māṣas, but one should not increase it further than that.
At the beginning, there are two *raktis*; when increasing the second [dose], there are three *raktis*;
and from that point onward, one should certainly increase by five *raktis* each time.
According to the Vātsarika-kalpa system,
one should decrease that [number of] days in reverse order during the remainder of the year by as many days as were increased at the beginning.
Of those eight māṣas, one should consume three in the morning,
two at midday, and the remaining two in the evening.
Thus, consuming that nectar, one obtains luster and a body that remains firm for a long time;
after merely three weeks, it destroys all diseases—what need is there to say more?
Here, by the ninety noble ones, the practice—free from ignorance, error, and doubt—has been correctly explained and elevated through sevenfold methods. (RCint 8.191)
Having reached the further shore of the treatises composed by the sages and having extracted their essence from them,
a certain practitioner of the six duties has composed this for the benefit of his kinsmen.
(Tāmrayoga) Having heated a copper leaf well twenty times in virgin water, one should throw it [into that liquid].
Then, having rubbed pure sulphur in two parts with lime juice, one should smear the copper leaves with it. RCint_8.193.
Having placed it in a vessel and sealed the vessel, one should cast it into the fire of a Śālā for five nights.
Once it has become cool, one should infuse it with the aforementioned waters, or else with water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā) for one day.
Having ground [the substance] with honey and clarified butter, one should roast it; thus purified, it becomes perfected for the attainment of bodily perfection.
One should consume a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed, combined with the juice of the *śālmalī* tree and taken with honey and clarified butter, for half a year.
One should prescribe milk or sugar as a post-digestive drink, along with food prepared with ghee or molasses mixed with sour substances;
this bestows vigor, nourishment, digestive fire, firmness of the body, divine vision, and long life.
In the *Tāmrayoga* (2):

mercury is twice the amount of copper, and black mica (*kṛṣṇābhraka*) is likewise twice the amount of copper. Each of these must be purified separately; thereafter, the purification of copper is of two kinds.
Likewise, the killing [of mercury] occurs through the application of sulfur to it when it has been made into a leaf, or by means of salts;
or when copper, having been smeared and heated, is immersed in a decoction of *nirguṇḍī* and fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
That which has the luster of red ochre should be ground with half its weight of sulfur;
subsequently, by means of *puṭapāka* (closed-oven heating), the mica (*abhraka*) becomes completely purified.
Then, having placed it in a lump of *hilamocī* root and smeared it inside a clay vessel,
one should burn the sharp [substance], grind it with sour water, and ensure it is well-mixed while avoiding exposure to moonlight.
The mercury, having been heated in a copper vessel and rubbed on a slab of khalvaśilā, should be formed into a ball;
then, after being steamed repeatedly with house-water and a paste of nirguṇḍī until it is purified, [it is ready]. RCint 8.201.
This triad of proven substances, combined separately with half a *karṣa* each of powdered copper,
long pepper (*pippalī*), viḍaṅga, and black pepper (*marica*), should be finely ground and consumed in a dose of two or three *māṣakas*.

This is a great elixir for diseases such as colic, acid dyspepsia, edema, malabsorption syndrome, consumption, and abdominal ailments; here, there is no restriction regarding dietary or behavioral prohibitions.
(Lakṣmīvilāsarasa):
One part of powdered black clouds (kṛṣṇābhra), half of that [part] each of mercury and sulfur,
half of that again of camphor, and likewise one part each of nutmeg and mace.
The seed of the *vṛddhadāraka* plant, the seed of the *unmattaka*, the seed of *trailokyavijayā*, and the tuber of the *vidārī* plant; RCint_8.205 //
Likewise, nārāyaṇī, nāgabalā, and atibalā;
also the seed of gokṣuraka and the seed of haijjala.
Having taken one karṣa of the powder of these [substances] and grinding it again with water,
pills should be prepared, measuring the size of three guñjā fruits.

It destroys diseases arising from the combination of the humors (sannipāta), as well as those that are terrible and most dreadful, whether they arise from wind (vāta) or bile (pitta); there is no restriction whatsoever in this regard.
The eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), as well as the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha),
fistula-in-ano (nāḍīvraṇa), severe ulcers (vraṇa), hemorrhoids (gudāmaya), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara).
Elephantiasis arising from phlegm and wind, chronic conditions inherited through family lineage, swelling of the throat, intestinal hernia, and most severe dysentery; RCint 8.210.
Cough, catarrh, consumption, hemorrhoids, obesity, and weakness; as well as rheumatism of every form, stiffness of the tongue, and constriction of the throat. RCint_8.211
It cures abdominal ailments, abnormalities of the ears, nose, eyes, and mouth, all types of colic, and headaches; it is a destroyer of diseases in women.
One should eat one pill daily every morning according to one's strength;
this is declared to be the accompanying vehicle (anupāna): minced meat, flour, milk, or curd.
By consuming fermented gruel, wine, and spirituous liquor, one assumes any form at will;
even an old man rivals the youth, and there is no depletion of semen.
There shall be no weakness of the sexual organ, nor do the hairs turn grey;
he may constantly approach a hundred women, possessing the prowess of an elephant in rut.
A vision extending for two hundred thousand yojanas arises;
this supreme rite of nourishment has been declared as the king of practices by the great-souled Nārada.
Rasa is the playfulness of Lakṣmī, which is Vāsudeva in the Teacher of the World;
through the practice of which the Blessed One becomes beloved among the women of Lakṣaṇā.
When the mountain minerals, such as gold and others, heated by the sun,
exude a substance that resembles lac, is soft, fine-textured, and clear, that impurity is called *śilājatu*.
Śilājatu is non-acidic, non-astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect.
Neither too hot nor too cold, its origin is from four elements:
gold, silver, copper, and even excellent black iron.
(Śilājatu: medicinal and physical properties derived from gold)
That which is sweet and slightly bitter, resembling the Japā flower,
pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold, is the exudation of gold.
(Śilājatu: medicinal and physical properties derived from silver)
That which originates from copper is pungent, white, cold, and sweet when digested.
(Śilājatu from copper: medicinal properties)
Copper (regarding its physical properties): resembling the throat of a peacock, it is bitter and hot, and it is digested as pungent.
(Śilājatu: derived from iron:: medicinal/physical properties)
That which resembles guggulu in appearance, is bitter, endowed with saltiness, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold, is the best of all; that is the iron [variety].
All those which have the scent of cow urine are suitable for all ritual applications;
however, in the practice of elixirs (*rasāyana*), the last one is distinguished as superior.
Respectively, for wind-pitta, pitta-śleṣman, and for the three [doshas] including kapha,
the impurities derived from metals such as gold and others are especially praised.

(Examination of Śilājatu: It behaves like iron dross in fire, burns without emitting smoke when placed in water, floats on the tip of a blade of grass, and sinks like a thread when placed below. RCint_8.225.
Whatever part of the bitumen (*śilājatu*) may be impure, one should wash it with pure water;
having placed it in iron vessels according to the prescribed method, one should collect that which has risen to the surface. *RCint_8.226*
When well-impregnated with decoctions that destroy wind, bile, and phlegm—
either all together or each one individually— it attains a supreme excellence of potency.
Having cast it out and drawn it up again, one should cast that [substance] back into the liquid;
by this method, its infusion (*bhāvanā*) should be performed for seven days while it is lukewarm.

An equal quantity of *girija* (bitumen) should be boiled with four times its measure of water along with the medicinal substance intended for infusion; then, when the decoction has been reduced to one-fourth and is pleasantly warm, one should add the *girija*.
Once it has reached a state of uniform consistency and has dried, one should throw it back again into the liquid.
(Śilājatu:
medicinal properties) According to the previously mentioned procedure, [it should be taken] together with iron powders.
When that [mixture] is drunk with milk, it bestows long life accompanied by happiness.

One who subsists on milk should employ that [practice], which is the supreme pacifier of old age and disease, the bringer of firmness to the body, the enhancer of intelligence and memory, and the source of prosperity. RCint_8.231
The application consists of three periods of seven days each and one period of seven days;
it is taught as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The dosage of śilājatu for medicinal use should be one pala, half a pala, or the smallest amount, one karṣa.
In the administration of *śilājatu*, one should avoid foods that cause burning sensations and those that are heavy.
One should avoid them at all times and should completely shun horse gram.

Sour milks, juices, broths, water with urine, and various decoctions are recommended for the purpose of dissolving the mineral; these should be employed after carefully considering the specific task at hand.
